data.title: Premarket: AI hardware stocks up 4.0%, Nvidia 2.9%; the four biggest spenders barely move
data.description:
Shares of the companies that make AI hardware, and of one that rents it out, rose in pre-market trading on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, after Nvidia reported revenue above its own forecast and its interim chief executive raised next year's growth target. At 4:27 a.m. Eastern, ten such stocks were up 4.0% on average, according to Nasdaq quotes. CoreWeave led with a gain of 6.7%.

Nvidia itself was up 2.9%. The four largest spenders on AI data centers barely moved: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were up 0.6% on average. On TECHi's calculation the typical stock in the hardware group had recovered 62% of what it lost over the previous two sessions, against 12% for the typical buyer. Pre-market trading is thin, and prices can change before the market opens at 9:30 a.m.

Which AI stocks are moving most?

The gains are widest among companies that sell the parts and the buildings of AI computing. CoreWeave, which rents out computing capacity built on Nvidia chips, was up 6.7% at $53.22. Dell, which builds AI servers, was up 4.7% at $338.00. Super Micro Computer, which builds AI servers, was up 4.3% at $25.18. Vertiv, which makes power and cooling equipment for data centers, was up 4.0% at $198.00. TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia and others, was up 4.0% at $374.00. Marvell, which designs custom and networking chips for data centers, was up 3.9% at $154.59. Micron, which makes memory chips, was up 3.8% at $739.55. Arista Networks, which sells data center networking gear, was up 3.4% at $192.74. AMD, which is Nvidia's main rival in AI chips, was up 3.1% at $519.00. Broadcom, which sells custom AI chips and networking chips, was up 2.4% at $349.88.

Oracle, which both buys Nvidia chips and sells cloud capacity, was up 2.5% after losing 8.3% in two sessions. Shares of TSMC here are its US-listed depositary shares. Pre-market trading on Nasdaq runs from 4 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. Eastern.

All ten fell over Monday and Tuesday, ahead of Tuesday evening's results. They lost 6.5% on average over the two sessions, and Nvidia lost 4.5%. Super Micro and TSMC fell about 10% each and Micron 8.5%. Broadcom held up best, down 1.6%.

The longer view is different, and it matters for reading Wednesday's prices. Since November 6, when Nvidia's slide began, Nvidia had fallen 17% by Tuesday's close. Over the same seven sessions Broadcom rose 16%, AMD 12%, Arista 9% and CoreWeave 8%. Investors had already been favoring some of the companies around Nvidia before the results arrived. Super Micro, down 16% over the same stretch, was not one of them.

Why would hardware makers gain more than Nvidia?

Nvidia's results were strong. Revenue for the quarter was $115.8 billion, $7.8 billion above the midpoint of its forecast, and Colette Kress, the interim chief executive, raised the growth forecast for next fiscal year to 75%, as TECHi reported on Tuesday evening. But four things in the documents point to the money flowing past Nvidia to the companies around it.

The first is what Nvidia has promised to buy. Its commentary shows supply commitments of $390 billion, up $111 billion in one quarter, mostly for memory chips. That is a multi-year order book for its suppliers, a point TECHi examined earlier on Wednesday. Micron's latest annual report shows $134 billion of contracted orders of its own.

The second is margin. Nvidia expects its gross margin to fall to between 71% and 72% this quarter from 74.8%. It has not said why. A lower margin on higher sales means a larger share of each dollar goes to someone else.

The third is who is buying. Nvidia splits its data center revenue into two groups. The largest cloud companies paid it $60.1 billion in the quarter, up 71% from a year earlier. Everyone else, a group Nvidia labels AI clouds, industrial and enterprise, paid $47.5 billion, up 195%. Nvidia's release names CoreWeave among the partners already running its new Rubin systems, and its commentary lists $32 billion of commitments under what it calls neocloud agreements.

The fourth is pace. Nvidia's forecast of $130.0 billion for the current quarter covers 14 weeks, and per week it is only 4.2% above last quarter, as TECHi's report on the results showed. The bigger growth it promises is a year away. The orders it has placed with suppliers are already signed.

Nvidia also carries a burden its suppliers do not. Its chairman said on Tuesday's call that the board will not bring back Jensen Huang, and it has only just hired a firm to find a permanent chief executive, according to reports of the call.

Why are the biggest buyers flat?

For Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, Nvidia's growth is a cost. The $60.1 billion that the largest cloud companies paid Nvidia last quarter works out to $4.6 billion a week. A forecast of 75% growth next year tells their shareholders the bill is still rising. Amazon was up 0.9% at $260.10. Alphabet was up 0.8% at $282.46. Microsoft was up 0.3% at $507.99. Meta was up 0.3% at $620.80.

They are also trying to shrink it. Microsoft used its Ignite conference on Tuesday to promote its own AI models and its own chip, as TECHi reported. Its latest quarterly report showed $39.4 billion spent on property and equipment in three months, about double the figure of a year earlier.

Nvidia, for its part, is giving some large customers longer to pay. Its receivables rose to 64 days of sales from 60, which it put down partly to extended payment terms on large agreements with certain customers.

There is a simpler reason too. The four fell less in the sell-off, 3.9% on average over two sessions against 6.5% for the hardware group, so they had less ground to make up.

How much of this week's loss is back?

Not all of it, for most. TECHi measured recovery as each stock's pre-market gain divided by its fall from Friday's close to Tuesday's close. Among the ten hardware stocks the median recovery was 62% by 4:27 a.m., meaning half had made back more than that and half less. CoreWeave and Broadcom had recovered all of their losses. TSMC, Super Micro Computer and Micron had recovered the least, between 37% and 41%.

Nvidia had recovered 61% of its two-session loss. At $159.95 it was still 14% below its close of $186.64 on November 6, where its recent slide began. The pre-market gain is worth about $109 billion of market value on Nvidia's diluted share count.

Among the four buyers the median recovery was 12%.

These are early prices. Trading before the open is thin, and Nvidia's gain was larger in Tuesday's after-hours session, when it rose about 4%. A stock that fell further also has more room to bounce, which flatters the hardware group. Nasdaq's pre-market quotes are last trades, and a single trade can move a quote. One snapshot does not settle which side of the AI trade investors prefer.

What to watch

The regular session opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, and the first hour will show whether the gap between hardware makers and buyers holds once volume arrives. Palo Alto Networks reports results after the close, according to Nasdaq's calendar. Nvidia's quarterly report is due by December 4, and Micron is due to report in December. The US chip export rule that China has promised to answer takes effect on Thursday, as TECHi reported. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and CoreWeave carry live prices.

data.title: Premarket: AI hardware stocks up 3.9%; Wednesday’s 4.0% early gain ended the day at 0.7%
data.description:
Stocks tied to AI hardware rose in pre-market trading on Thursday, November 19, 2026, hours before Anthropic's shares are due to begin trading. At 6:14 a.m. Eastern the ten hardware stocks TECHi tracks were up 3.9% on average, according to Nasdaq quotes. CoreWeave and Micron led with gains of 5.4%. Nvidia was up 2.1%.

Wednesday is the reason to be careful with that number. The same ten stocks were up 4.0% before the open a day earlier, after Nvidia reported results above its own forecast, and they finished the session up 0.7%. On TECHi's calculation 83% of the early gain was gone by the close. Nvidia itself turned a 2.9% pre-market rise into a 2.9% fall.

Which AI stocks are moving?

The gains are broad. Every one of the ten hardware stocks was higher, and so were the four largest spenders on AI data centers.

CoreWeave, which rents out computing capacity built on Nvidia chips, was up 5.4% at $50.41. Micron, which makes memory chips, was up 5.4% at $743.31. Super Micro Computer, which builds AI servers, was up 4.6% at $25.48. Marvell, which designs custom and networking chips for data centers, was up 4.5% at $152.06. Dell, which builds AI servers, was up 4.3% at $326.80. Vertiv, which makes power and cooling equipment for data centers, was up 3.9% at $202.13. Arista Networks, which sells data center networking gear, was up 3.5% at $200.74. AMD, which is Nvidia's main rival in AI chips, was up 3.2% at $547.05. Broadcom, which sells custom AI chips and networking chips, was up 3.1% at $364.99. TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia and others, was up 1.2% at $366.89.

Among the spenders, the moves were Alphabet 4.1%, Amazon 2.6%, Meta 1.5% and Microsoft 1.3%. Before the open on Wednesday the four were up 0.6% on average. On Thursday morning they were up 2.4%.

Alphabet has a direct interest in the day's main event. Its Google unit agreed to buy about $10.0 billion of Anthropic stock in a private sale alongside the public offering, Anthropic's prospectus says. Anthropic priced its shares at $83 on Wednesday evening, above its range, as TECHi reported overnight. Reuters reported that Nasdaq futures rose on hopes for a strong debut.

Oracle, which both buys Nvidia chips and sells cloud capacity, was up 2.6%. Shares of TSMC here are its US-listed depositary shares. Pre-market trading on Nasdaq runs from 4 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. Eastern, and volumes are a fraction of a normal session.

What happened to Wednesday's early gains?

Most of them faded. TECHi recorded the same group at 4:27 a.m. on Wednesday and published the result. The ten hardware stocks were up 4.0% on average and all ten were higher.

By the 4 p.m. close the average gain was 0.7%. Four of the ten ended the day lower: CoreWeave, Dell, Marvell and Micron. Only three finished above where they stood before the open. Those were AMD, Broadcom and Arista Networks. Four kept at least half of their early gain.

Nvidia was the clearest case. It was up 2.9% before the open and closed down 2.9%, at its lowest closing price since June 2025, as TECHi reported on Wednesday. The same report found that Nvidia has closed below its opening price on the day after nine of its last ten earnings releases.

The spenders went the other way. They were up 0.6% before Wednesday's open and ended the day up 1.2%. Amazon went from a 0.9% early gain to a 3.8% rise at the close. Alphabet held its 0.8%, Microsoft finished up 0.4%, and Meta slipped from a small gain to a loss of 0.4%.

The reversals were large. CoreWeave went from a gain of 6.7% before the open to a loss of 4.1% at the close. Dell went from 4.7% up to 2.9% down, Marvell from 3.9% up to 2.2% down, and Micron from 3.8% up to 1.0% down. TSMC and Super Micro Computer each gave back more than three points and finished about 1% higher. AMD, Broadcom and Arista Networks did the opposite and added to their early gains, with AMD ending the day up 5.3%.

Thursday's rebound is strongest where Wednesday's selling was. All four hardware stocks that closed lower on Wednesday are among the five biggest pre-market gainers.

Where does each stock stand for the week?

Still lower, for most. The group fell hard over the first three sessions of the week. From Friday's close to Wednesday's, the ten hardware stocks lost 5.8% on average. CoreWeave, Micron, Super Micro Computer, TSMC and Dell each lost about 9%.

Thursday's pre-market gains repair part of that. On average the five have recovered 40% of the three-day loss. Measured against last Friday's close, the ten hardware stocks were down 2.2% on average at Thursday's pre-market prices. The four spenders were down 0.4%.

Four of the fifteen stocks in the table were above Friday's close: Broadcom by 5.2%, Amazon by 3.0%, AMD by 2.4% and Arista Networks by 1.7%. Vertiv was level with Friday's close. TSMC was furthest below, down 8.0%.

Nvidia was 5.4% below Friday's close of $162.85. From its pre-market price of $154.09 it would need to rise another 5.7% to get back there.

Why is Nvidia lagging again?

Its 2.1% gain put it near the bottom of the group. Only TSMC had gained less. That was also the pattern on Wednesday morning, when Nvidia's rise was smaller than the average for the companies that supply it and compete with it.

Nvidia has fallen in seven of the eight sessions since November 6 and has lost 19.1% over that stretch, while AMD has gained 18.1%.

The reasons investors give have not changed. Nvidia has an interim chief executive and a board that is searching for a permanent one. A US rule limiting exports of advanced AI chips takes effect on Thursday, and Nvidia has stopped selling its H200 chips to China, as TECHi reported earlier on Thursday.

The price reflects it. At $154.09, Nvidia trades at 9.9 times the earnings analysts expect for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, on Nasdaq's consensus of $15.55 a share.

There is a case for the other side. Nvidia's revenue was $115.8 billion last quarter and it forecast $130 billion for this one. At under ten times next year's expected earnings, the stock is priced for little of that growth.

Will the gains hold this time?

Wednesday's record says not to assume so. The early gain then was bigger, it followed results that beat forecasts, and it mostly disappeared.

A simple marker follows from that record. If the hardware group keeps half of Thursday's early gain, it will close up about 2.0%. On Wednesday it kept about a sixth.

There is one difference. Wednesday's rise was a reaction to a single company's report. Thursday's comes with a new stock arriving. Anthropic's listing is the largest on record, according to Reuters, and seven chip and cloud companies are buying $26.0 billion of its stock in the private sale. How the shares trade will be read as a verdict on demand for AI itself.

What to watch

The regular session opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern. Anthropic's first trade is expected later in the day, under the symbol ANT. The comparison to make at 4 p.m. is the one TECHi made on Wednesday: how much of the morning's gain is left. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and Alphabet carry live prices.

data.title: Coherent sets $2 billion buyback, the same sum Nvidia paid for its stake in March
data.description:
Coherent Corp.'s board has authorized the company to buy back up to $2.0 billion of its own stock, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The program has no end date and does not oblige the company to buy a single share. Coherent's stock was up 10.1% at $234.27 at 9:56 a.m. Eastern, about twice the gain of other makers of optical parts for AI data centers.

The figure has a counterpart. In March, Nvidia paid $2.0 billion for 7.79 million new Coherent shares at $256.80 each. Coherent closed at $212.84 on Wednesday, 17% below that price. At Wednesday's close the same $2.0 billion would buy 9.40 million shares, 1.6 million more than the company issued to Nvidia, TECHi's calculation shows. There is a complication. Coherent's operations and capital spending together used $868 million of cash in its latest quarter, and the company holds less unrestricted cash than the full program would cost.

What did Coherent announce?

The filing is three paragraphs long. It says the board authorized the program on Wednesday, November 18, and that the company may repurchase up to $2.0 billion of its common stock, not counting fees and commissions.

It gives the company a wide choice of methods. Purchases can be made in the open market, in negotiated deals including accelerated buybacks, in block trades through a broker, under pre-arranged trading plans, or by selling put options and using other derivatives.

It also sets out how little is promised. The program has no expiration date. It does not oblige Coherent to buy any particular number of shares, and it may be suspended or stopped at any time.

The filing does not say why the board acted now, how purchases will be paid for or when they will begin. It is signed by the chief financial officer, Sherri Luther, and has no press release attached.

Coherent makes lasers and optical components. Most of its revenue now comes from its data center and communications business, which includes the optical parts that move data between servers in AI data centers. The quarterly report it filed on November 4 makes no mention of a repurchase program. The only shares the company took in last quarter were about 435,000 withheld from employees to cover tax on stock awards, at a cost of $128.6 million.

How much stock would $2 billion buy?

That depends on the price, and the price has moved a long way this year.

At Wednesday's close of $212.84, $2.0 billion buys 9.40 million shares. Coherent had 196.96 million shares outstanding on November 2, so that is 4.8% of the company.

The same sum would have bought far less in June. Coherent's highest close of the past year was $426.89 on June 2. By Wednesday the stock had halved. At the June price, $2.0 billion covered 4.69 million shares, or 2.4%.

The low since that peak came this month. Coherent fell 13% on November 5, the day after it reported quarterly results, to close at $169.76. It had recovered 25% from there by Wednesday.

A buyback would also offset some recent dilution. Coherent had about 155.6 million shares outstanding at the end of June 2025 and 196.9 million at the end of September 2026, an increase of 27%. Most of that came from 30.1 million shares issued when preferred stock was converted late last year and from the shares sold to Nvidia. The full program, spent at Wednesday's price, would reverse a little under a quarter of the increase.

Why does the Nvidia sale matter?

Because it was the same amount of money going the other way, at a higher price.

On March 2, Coherent sold 7,788,161 new shares to Nvidia at $256.80 each, for $2.0 billion in cash. The sale came with a multi-year supply agreement, including what the companies called a multi-billion-dollar purchase commitment from Nvidia. Coherent said the money would support research, new capacity and its operations as it expands manufacturing in the United States. Its shares rose 15% that day.

Nvidia still held every one of those shares on September 30, according to its latest holdings report, which valued them at $2.24 billion. A six-month restriction on selling them has ended. The purchase agreement also contained what Coherent calls a price protection provision, which ran for six months. The quarterly report says it expired in September without being triggered.

Since then the price has dropped below what Nvidia paid. Coherent last closed above $256.80 on October 14. At Wednesday's close the stake was worth $1.66 billion, $342 million less than it cost.

That gap is the arithmetic in favor of the board's decision. Coherent issued 7.79 million shares for $2.0 billion. If it spent $2.0 billion at Wednesday's price it would retire 9.40 million. The company would have taken in and paid out the same sum and ended, all else equal, with 1.6 million fewer shares than it had before the Nvidia deal.

Two cautions apply. The filing does not connect the program to Nvidia's money, and that money was raised to pay for expansion. And the sum only works below $256.80. Thursday's rise moved the stock closer to that level.

Can Coherent afford it?

Not from the cash it held at the end of September, if it also keeps building at the present rate.

Business is strong. Revenue in the three months to September 30 was $2.37 billion, up 50% from a year earlier. Sales to data center and communications customers rose 79% to $1.95 billion and made up 82% of the total. Net earnings were $384.7 million, or $1.90 a share.

Cash moved the other way. Coherent's operations used $92.7 million in the quarter, and the largest single item was a $737 million increase in inventory. Capital spending was $775.5 million, more than seven times the $103.9 million of a year earlier. Together that is an outflow of $868 million.

The company covered it in two ways. Subsidiaries outside the United States borrowed $773 million under new local credit lines, and Coherent ran down its short-term investments by $625 million.

At the end of September it had $1.55 billion of cash and $200 million of short-term investments, or $1.75 billion in all. A further $583 million was restricted. Total debt was $4.00 billion, up from $3.22 billion three months earlier.

So the program is larger than the unrestricted cash Coherent held. It equals a little more than five quarters of net earnings at the latest rate. Unless cash flow turns, buying the full amount would mean borrowing more or buying slowly. The absence of an end date allows for the second.

Management expects the business to keep growing. On November 4 it forecast revenue of $2.55 billion to $2.75 billion for the current quarter and said it expects its first $3 billion quarter by the end of its fiscal year next June.

How did the stock react?

Coherent was at $234.27 at 9:56 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, up 10.1% from Wednesday's close, according to Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data. That adds about $4.2 billion to the company's market value, 2.1 times the size of the program.

Not all of that is the buyback. AI hardware stocks rose broadly on Thursday morning, as TECHi reported before the open. Lumentum, Coherent's closest listed rival in optical components, was up 5.1% at about the same time. Ciena was up 5.5% and Nvidia 2.9%. Coherent's gain was roughly 5 points more than the two optical companies'.

The move takes the stock back to about where it stood a week ago. It closed at $234.51 on November 11 and was 13% lower by November 16, a stretch in which AI stocks fell after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, as TECHi reported.

At Thursday morning's price the arithmetic above is a little weaker. $2.0 billion buys 8.54 million shares at $234.27, 0.7 million more than Nvidia received. Nvidia's stake is worth $1.82 billion, $175 million below its cost.

There is a case on each side. The stock is still 45% below its June high after Thursday's rise while revenue has grown by half, the share count is a quarter higher than in mid-2025, and the board is signalling that it sees value at this price. Against that, an authorization is not a purchase. The company is spending more than it earns on factories and inventory, its debt rose by $778 million in a single quarter, and money spent on shares is not available for expansion.

One further fact bears on how the program will be judged. In August the board's compensation committee granted special stock awards to senior executives, among them one with a target value of $50 million for chief executive Jim Anderson. They vest only if the share price reaches set milestones and other conditions are met through 2030, a company filing shows.

What to watch

Coherent's next quarterly report, due around early February, has to show how many shares it bought and at what average price. Free cash flow for the December quarter will show whether the outflow is narrowing. Nvidia's next holdings report, in mid-February, will show whether it still owns its 7.79 million shares. The method matters too: an accelerated buyback retires a large block at once, while open-market buying can take years. TECHi's Coherent quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia rules out Huang’s return and lifts growth target to 75%; that needs 18% a quarter
data.description:
Nvidia's board does not intend to bring Jensen Huang back as chief executive, chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of the company's earnings call on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, according to CNBC and CBS News. On the same call, held after Nvidia reported its results, interim chief executive Colette Kress raised the company's revenue growth forecast for its next fiscal year to 75% from 70%.

The forecast is larger than it sounds. On TECHi's calculation it puts revenue for the year to January 2028 at about $741 billion, which is $318 billion more than this year. To get there from the quarter Nvidia has just guided, sales would have to grow about 18% every quarter. The outlook for the current quarter implies 4%. Nvidia shares were up about 4% in after-hours trading.

What did the board say about Jensen Huang?

Jones, the board's new chairman, opened the call himself. Huang's resignation was announced on November 12. CNBC quoted Jones as saying the board had accepted it unanimously and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO". CBS News reported the same statement.

He also gave the first detail on what comes next. The board has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief executive, CNBC reported. It is considering candidates from inside and outside the company and has every confidence in Kress in the meantime, according to CBS News.

Jones did not take questions on the circumstances of the resignation or on the board's investigation, and said the board would say more when appropriate, Scripps News reported. None of the accounts of the call reports a date for an appointment.

The statement came hours after Huang said publicly that he would return if the board decided it was in the company's interest, CBS News reported. The board's answer was no.

Kress, for her part, told analysts that the business is running as usual and that customers, suppliers and partners are behind the company, according to Scripps News. Analysts cited by CNBC said the financial effect of the change at the top is unlikely to show before the end of fiscal 2028, because most of next year's revenue is already under contract.

That settles one of the two things Nvidia's results release and written commentary left open. TECHi's report on the results noted that they gave no update on the investigation and no timetable for a successor. The call added a search firm. The accounts of it do not include a timetable.

What did Kress forecast?

The quarter she reported was strong. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and $7.8 billion above the midpoint of Nvidia's own forecast. Nvidia formally guides one quarter at a time, and for the current quarter it expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%.

On the call Kress went further. Investors had wondered whether Nvidia would drop an earlier forecast of 70% growth for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, CNBC reported. She raised it to 75%. She tied her confidence to supply, saying the chips, the advanced packaging and the memory Nvidia needs are all coming together.

Other details come from news accounts of the call. A transcript was not yet available on Tuesday evening. Kress pointed to a backlog of $2.5 trillion across the cloud industry, up from $2 trillion three months ago, and said contracts for Nvidia's older Hopper chips are being renewed at up to twice their original prices, according to investingLive. She said Nvidia intends to return all of its excess free cash flow to shareholders. The product schedule is unchanged, with the next version of its Rubin systems due next year and a new design called Feynman in 2028, the same account says.

On the chip export rule the Commerce Department issued on Monday, Kress said Nvidia would study it and that demand still far exceeds supply, CBS News reported. Nvidia put the small fall in its gross margin last quarter down to the start of production of its Rubin chips, as its written commentary had said. TECHi has not seen a reason given for the larger fall it forecasts.

What does 75% growth require?

Start with this year. Nvidia has reported $293.7 billion of revenue for the first nine months of fiscal 2027. Add the $130.0 billion it expects this quarter and the year comes to $423.7 billion. That is 96% more than the $215.9 billion of fiscal 2026.

Growth of 75% on top of that is $741 billion. The step up from 70% to 75% is worth about $21 billion by itself. In dollars it would be the biggest increase Nvidia has ever attempted: $318 billion in one year, against $208 billion this year. Nvidia grew 65% in fiscal 2026. A 75% year would be slower than this one in percentage terms and far bigger in money. It works out to an average of $185 billion a quarter, 60% more than the record quarter Nvidia reported on Tuesday.

The calendar makes the task slightly harder. Fiscal 2027 has 53 weeks and fiscal 2028 has 52. Per week, the forecast is growth of 78%.

The harder part is the starting point. The current quarter's outlook works out to $9.29 billion a week, or $120.7 billion for a normal 13-week quarter. As TECHi showed earlier on Tuesday, that is only 4.2% above last quarter's weekly rate. If Nvidia kept growing at 4.2% a quarter, fiscal 2028 would come to about $536 billion, an increase of 26%.

To reach $741 billion, revenue has to grow 17.9% in each of the next four quarters. That would take quarterly revenue from the equivalent of $120.7 billion now to $233 billion in the final quarter of fiscal 2028. Nvidia has done it before. It grew 18% in the second quarter of this year and 20% in the third. The forecast says, in effect, that the slower quarter it has just guided is the exception.

A better current quarter would help only a little. Nvidia beat its last forecast by 7.3%. If it did the same again, this year's total would rise too, and the growth needed each quarter would still be 15.8%.

What does it mean for Nvidia stock?

Nvidia closed on Tuesday at $155.46, before the results. In the six sessions to Monday, the shares had lost about $735 billion of market value, as TECHi reported on Tuesday morning. At that price the company is worth about $3.76 trillion on its diluted share count, or five times the revenue the new forecast implies for fiscal 2028.

The case for the stock is that the forecast was raised in the same week the founder left, and that Kress backed it with supply contracts and a promise of more cash for shareholders. By Kress's account, customers are paying more for old chips, not less.

The case against is everything the call did not resolve. Nvidia has an interim chief executive, a search that has only just started and an investigation its chairman will not discuss. Its quarterly report has not been filed. A new export rule is days old. And a full-year forecast given on a call is not the same as guidance, which Nvidia still gives for one quarter only.

What to watch

The quarterly report is due by December 4 and is where Nvidia must describe legal proceedings. Huang has agreed to appear before House lawmakers on December 1, CBS News reported. The next results, expected in late February, bring the first test. A first-quarter outlook near $142 billion would be on the path to 75%. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Everpure revenue jumps 51%, $125M above its forecast; inventory is up fivefold this year
data.description:
Everpure, the data storage company formerly called Pure Storage, reported revenue of $1.46 billion for the three months to November 1, 2026, up 51% from a year earlier, according to results released after the market closed on Wednesday, November 18. That is $125 million above the top of the range the company gave in August. It raised its full-year forecast for the third quarter in a row.

Two details sit behind the headline. Most of the raise is revenue already earned: $130 million of the $155 million added to the full-year midpoint is the amount by which the latest quarter beat its forecast, TECHi's calculation shows. And the growth is absorbing cash. Inventory has grown fivefold since the fiscal year began, to $379 million. The shares rose as much as 6.6% in after-hours trading and were up 2.5% around 5:23 p.m. Eastern.

How did Everpure do against its forecast?

It beat both of the measures it guides. In August the company told investors to expect revenue of $1.325 billion to $1.335 billion and adjusted operating income of $265 million to $275 million. Revenue came in at $1.46 billion. Adjusted operating income was $345 million, $70 million above the top of its range.

Product revenue, which is the sale of storage systems, was $948 million, up 77%. Subscription services revenue was $512 million, up 19%. Annual recurring revenue from subscriptions reached $2.2 billion, up 20%. Remaining performance obligations, the value of contracts not yet counted as revenue, were $4.2 billion, up 44%.

Net income was $100.4 million, or 29 cents a share, against $54.8 million, or 16 cents, a year earlier.

Growth has been speeding up for more than two years. In August Everpure said its revenue growth had accelerated for eight quarters in a row. The latest quarter makes nine. The last five readings are 16%, 20%, 35%, 38% and now 51%.

The company tied part of that to AI. It said it has won a design contract with a second of the five largest hyperscale cloud companies, and that its FlashBlade//EXA system ranked first on every checkpointing and cache measure submitted in MLPerf Storage v3.0, an industry benchmark built around AI workloads. Everpure joined the S&P 500 in September.

What does the new forecast imply?

For the current quarter, which ends around the end of January, Everpure expects revenue of $1.50 billion to $1.52 billion and adjusted operating income of $350 million to $360 million. For the full fiscal year it now expects revenue of $5.20 billion to $5.21 billion, up from $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion, and adjusted operating income of $1.08 billion to $1.09 billion, up from $940 million to $960 million.

The midpoint of the revenue forecast rose by $155 million. The quarter just reported beat the midpoint of its own forecast by $130 million. So 84% of the raise is money that has already come in.

The rest is the change to the quarter ahead. The old full-year forecast left about $1.48 billion for the fourth quarter, on TECHi's arithmetic. The new midpoint is $1.51 billion, about 2% higher.

That forecast also implies a slowdown. Revenue of $1.51 billion would be 3.4% more than the quarter just reported, which was itself 23% more than the one before. Measured against a year earlier it is growth of 42% to 43%, down from 51%. If that is what happens, it ends the run of acceleration.

Everpure's recent record suggests the range is cautious. To keep growth above 51%, it would need fourth-quarter revenue of about $1.60 billion, which is $83 million above the top of the new range. It beat the top of its range by $125 million this quarter and by $81 million in the quarter before.

Chief financial officer Tarek Robbiati said in the release that the company is also standing by a preliminary outlook for the fiscal year after this one. The release does not give those figures.

Where is the cash going?

Into components. Everpure builds its systems around flash memory. The company said in its quarterly report in September that components had become scarce and more costly, and that it raised its own prices in the first half of the fiscal year in response.

The cost shows in the margin. Gross margin was 68.0%, down from 72.3% a year earlier. On product sales alone it was 66.7%, against 71.6%, TECHi's calculation from the income statement shows. The cost of product revenue more than doubled while product revenue rose 77%.

The trend within the year is better. Product gross margin was 64.5% in the first quarter and 65.3% in the second before reaching 66.7%, which suggests the price increases are catching up with costs.

The larger effect is on the balance sheet. Inventory was $379.5 million on November 1. Three months earlier it was $106.3 million, and at the start of the fiscal year it was $75.9 million. Building it took $272 million of cash in the quarter.

A second line has grown as well. Prepaid expenses and other current assets stood at $967 million, against $356 million when the year began. The release does not break that down. In the September report most of the equivalent balance, $904 million of $1.03 billion, was money owed mainly by Everpure's contract manufacturers for components that Everpure bought itself and sold on to them, together with tax-related receivables. In other words the company has been buying parts itself and passing them to the manufacturers that assemble its systems.

Inventory and that line together come to $1.35 billion, $915 million more than at the start of the year. Part of that is unpaid bills, as accounts payable rose by $325 million. Cash and marketable securities fell to $1.14 billion from $1.55 billion.

Free cash flow recovered in the quarter, to $265 million from an outflow of $238 million in the one before. Over nine months it is $139 million, against $414 million in the same period last year, while revenue rose 42%. Capital spending in the quarter was $178 million, close to three times the level of a year earlier.

Everpure is not alone in committing cash to secure parts. Nvidia's supply commitments have reached $390 billion, most of it for memory, as TECHi reported earlier on Wednesday.

How did the stock react?

Unevenly. Everpure closed at $101.00 on Wednesday, down 0.8%, before the results. In after-hours trading it rose as high as $107.70 at 4:12 p.m. Eastern, a gain of 6.6%, according to Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data. Around 5:23 p.m. it was near $103.53, up 2.5%. After-hours trading is thin, and the company's call with analysts began at 5 p.m. Eastern. This report does not include it.

The stock's history after results is a warning against reading much into the first move. Everpure fell the day after each of its last four reports, by 27.3% last December, 10.3% in February, 14.8% in May and 8.9% in August, Nasdaq prices show. Each of those releases also said results had exceeded the top of the company's guidance.

The shares are still up 51% this year. They are 36% below their closing high of $156.97, set on October 13. At Wednesday's close the company was worth about $35 billion on its diluted share count. That is 6.8 times the revenue it forecasts for this fiscal year and about 33 times its forecast adjusted operating income.

There is a case on each side. Growth has accelerated for nine quarters, recurring revenue is $2.2 billion, and two of the largest cloud companies have chosen its technology. Against that, margins are lower than a year ago, cash is tied up in parts, and the forecast points to slower growth.

What to watch

Everpure's quarterly report, due in the coming weeks, will show what is inside its inventory and receivables. The fourth quarter will show whether revenue lands near the $1.51 billion it forecast or the $1.60 billion that would keep growth accelerating. Component prices will decide how much of that revenue it keeps as margin. TECHi's Everpure quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Cantor Fitzgerald’s Nvidia shares fell 45% last quarter; puts covered more than it held
data.description:
Cantor Fitzgerald reported owning 1.0 million Nvidia shares at the end of September, 45% fewer than three months earlier, according to the quarterly holdings report the firm filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 16, 2026. The same filing lists put options covering 1.3 million Nvidia shares, which is more than the stock it held.

The figures matter this week. House Democrats have asked Cantor whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose sons control the firm, used his office to help it avoid losses tied to Nvidia, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Cantor denies it. TECHi read four quarters of the firm's filings. They show a holding that is two-thirds smaller than at the start of the year and was matched by put options throughout. They do not show anything after September 30, and Nvidia's fall came after that date.

What are lawmakers asking?

Three House Democrats wrote to Brandon Lutnick, Cantor's chairman and the commerce secretary's son, on November 17, according to Reuters, which reviewed the letter. The three are Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

They asked for information to establish whether any of the secretary's actions were improperly influenced by Cantor's holdings or business interests, Reuters reported. The letter asks about one decision in particular: what the lawmakers describe as the secretary's refusal to add a Chinese company called Megaspeed to the trade blacklist, or to require a license for exports of advanced AI chips to it. Megaspeed has been in the spotlight since reports about its links to Nvidia's former chief executive, Jensen Huang, Reuters said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this month that four government agencies had favored listing the company and that the Commerce Department had not, according to the same report.

Both sides have answered. A Commerce Department spokesperson said the secretary has fully complied with his ethics agreement and has divested all of his financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald and two related companies, Reuters reported. Cantor denied the lawmakers' claims. It said it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia, that its Nvidia holdings arise mainly from equity swaps carried out for clients, and that it has no role in export control decisions.

The pressure is not from one party. Senator Tim Scott, the Republican who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, said he wants Lutnick and Huang to testify in public, according to Reuters.

What do Cantor's filings show?

Large investment managers must report their holdings of US-listed stocks to the SEC within 45 days of the end of each quarter, on a document called Form 13F. Cantor Fitzgerald, L.P. files one report for the group. Almost all of the Nvidia stock in it sits in a unit called CF Secured.

At the end of 2025 the group reported 3,000,419 Nvidia shares, worth $559.6 million. Three months later it reported 1,778,504. At the end of June the figure was 1,810,531. At the end of September it was 1,000,332, worth $228.5 million.

So the holding fell 45% in the third quarter, and it has fallen by two-thirds since the end of last year. The largest cut, 1.22 million shares, came in the first three months of 2026. The third-quarter cut was 810,199 shares.

The September holding was 2.2% of the $10.4 billion of positions in Cantor's report.

Did Cantor sell before Nvidia fell?

The filings cannot say, and the dates do not line up the way that question assumes.

The reduction the latest filing shows took place between July and September. Nvidia's shares rose 14% in those three months, closing at $228.38 on September 30. Whatever left Cantor's books in the quarter left while the price was climbing.

The fall came later. Nvidia's highest close was $239.24 on October 6. It closed at $150.96 on Wednesday, November 18, which is 37% below that peak and 34% below the September 30 price. Huang's resignation was announced on November 12.

A 13F is a photograph of one day. The September report says what Cantor held on September 30. It says nothing about October or November. The next one, covering December 31, is due in mid-February.

One calculation gives the scale of what is at issue. If Cantor still held the 1.0 million shares it reported, and nothing offset them, they would have been worth $151 million at Wednesday's close, $77 million less than on September 30. Neither condition is known.

What do the put options show?

A put option gives its holder the right to sell a share at a set price. On a 13F, options are listed by the value of the shares they cover and not by what the options cost. Cantor's report shows puts over 1.3 million Nvidia shares, which appears as $296.9 million. That is the share price multiplied by 1.3 million. It is not money spent or money at risk.

The puts are not new. Cantor reported puts over 4.55 million Nvidia shares at the end of 2025, 1.5 million in March and 1.4 million in June. At two of the four quarter-ends, including the latest, the puts covered more shares than the group held. At the other two they covered about four-fifths.

Someone who owns a stock and holds puts over a similar number of shares is largely protected if the price falls. That is also what a dealer's books look like when it holds shares to back contracts with clients and hedges them. Cantor says its Nvidia holdings come mainly from equity swaps for clients. In a swap of that kind the client takes the gain or the loss, and the dealer holds stock so that it is not exposed.

The filings fit that account. They cannot prove it. A 13F does not show swaps, short positions, or the price and expiry date of an option. It lists positions, and a list of positions is not a firm's net exposure.

What can't the filings answer?

The main one. Whether any decision at the Commerce Department was shaped by Cantor's interests is not something a holdings report can show, and nothing in these filings bears on it.

They also cannot show who Cantor's clients are, whether the firm carried any of the risk itself, or what it did after September 30. The lawmakers have asked Cantor for that kind of information directly.

What the filings do establish is narrower. Cantor's reported Nvidia stock fell in two of the last three quarters, by two-thirds in all. The fall began in the first quarter of the year. And at every date the stock was paired with put options of similar size.

What does it mean for Nvidia stock?

For shareholders the inquiry is one more source of scrutiny on a company that already has several. A US rule limiting exports of advanced AI chips took effect on Thursday, and Nvidia has stopped selling its H200 chips to China, as TECHi reported earlier on Thursday. Its board has set up a committee to oversee export controls and is searching for a permanent chief executive.

The question lawmakers are pressing is about enforcement. If the Commerce Department is pushed to act on Megaspeed or on other buyers, the effect on Nvidia would come through its sales and not through anything in Cantor's filings.

What to watch

Cantor's reply to the lawmakers, and whether they publish it. Any decision on adding Megaspeed to the trade blacklist. Hearings, if Scott's call for public testimony is taken up. Cantor's next holdings report, in mid-February, will show its position at the end of a quarter in which Nvidia has so far fallen by a third. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia’s supply commitments hit $390B, mostly memory; Micron’s margin now tops Nvidia’s
data.description:
Nvidia's commitments to its suppliers rose to $390 billion at the end of October from $279 billion three months earlier, mainly to secure memory chips for several years, according to the commentary it filed with its results on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. At the end of April the figure was $119 billion.

The other side of that bill shows up at Micron, the largest US maker of memory chips. Micron's latest quarter carried a gross margin of 86.8%, against 74.8% at Nvidia, and Nvidia has just forecast that its own margin will fall. TECHi's comparison of the two companies' filings shows the supplier now keeps more of each dollar of sales than its famous customer, and its shares cost about half as much relative to earnings.

What did Nvidia commit to?

Nvidia's finance team writes a commentary with each set of results. This one says the company has worked with its suppliers to secure the components it needs to meet demand for the next several years. Supply commitments rose from $279 billion to $390 billion in the quarter, mostly for multi-year purchases of memory.

The quarter before told the same story with a bigger number. Commitments jumped from $119 billion to $279 billion, again mainly for memory, Nvidia's August commentary said. That is $271 billion of new commitments in six months.

Set against the business, the pace is striking. The latest increase of $111 billion works out to $8.5 billion of new commitments a week, almost as much as the $8.9 billion a week Nvidia took in as revenue. The $390 billion total is more than 13 times what Nvidia spent on the products it sold last quarter, or over three years of costs at the current rate.

Nvidia has a reason to buy ahead. Its interim chief executive, Colette Kress, told analysts on Tuesday that she expects sales to grow 75% next fiscal year and tied that confidence to supply, as TECHi reported on Tuesday evening. The same commentary also notes a side effect: higher memory prices are hurting demand for consumer PCs.

What does it look like from Micron's side?

Micron's annual report, for the year that ended on September 3, reads like the mirror image. Revenue was $133.2 billion, up from $37.4 billion a year earlier. Micron says the average price of its main product, DRAM, rose about 180% while the amount it shipped grew by about a quarter. Demand from AI data centers, it says, is growing faster than the industry can add supply.

The more telling change is in how it sells. Micron now signs what it calls strategic customer agreements. Customers commit to buy fixed volumes over several years on a take-or-pay basis, in most cases at prices that move within an agreed floor and ceiling. They also put up security. Micron received $12.75 billion of cash deposits from customers during the year, most of it repayable between 2029 and 2031, and has $7 billion of letters of credit issued or promised.

Those contracts have built a backlog. Micron reports about $134 billion of orders still to be delivered under them, valued at the lowest prices the contracts allow. It expects to book a quarter of that as revenue within a year. A year earlier the figure was too small to disclose.

Micron does not say that Nvidia is one of those customers, and Nvidia does not name its suppliers. Micron's report says no single customer reached 10% of its revenue last year, though its ten largest together made up about half. The arithmetic shows why Nvidia's bill must be spread widely. The $111 billion Nvidia added in one quarter equals 83% of everything Micron sold in a year. Nvidia's total of $390 billion is almost three times Micron's whole contracted backlog. Even if every one of Micron's contracts were with Nvidia, most of Nvidia's commitments would have to sit elsewhere, with Micron's Korean rivals SK Hynix and Samsung and with suppliers of other parts.

Who keeps more of each dollar?

For most of the AI boom the answer was Nvidia. It is now Micron.

In its latest quarter Micron kept 86.8 cents of each dollar of sales after the cost of making its chips. Nvidia kept 74.8 cents. After operating expenses the gap is wider: 80.7 cents at Micron against 66.9 cents at Nvidia. On net income it is 69.5 cents against 56.4.

A year ago the positions were reversed. Micron's gross margin was 44.7% and Nvidia's was 73.4%.

The forecasts point the same way. Nvidia expects a gross margin between 71.0% and 72.0% this quarter, down from 74.8%. On revenue of $130.0 billion, those 3.3 points are worth about $4.3 billion of gross profit in a single quarter. Micron's forecast for its current quarter is a margin of about 86% on revenue of $61.5 billion.

Nvidia has not said why its margin will fall, as TECHi noted in its report on the results. So the filings do not prove that memory is the reason. They do show that Nvidia is paying more for it and committing to buy far more of it, and that the company selling it is earning more than ever.

How do the two stocks compare?

Micron closed on Tuesday at $712.42. That is up 150% this year and 41% below its closing high of $1,213.56 on June 25. It fell 7.6% on Monday alone. At Tuesday's price the company is worth about $806 billion, which is 9.6 times the $74.33 a share it earned last fiscal year. For the current quarter alone Micron forecasts earnings of about $37.84 a share, just over half of what it earned in all of last year.

Nvidia closed at $155.46, its lowest close in a year and down 17% in 2026, before rising about 4% in after-hours trading on its results. At the closing price it is worth about $3.76 trillion on its diluted share count, or 16.7 times its earnings of $9.31 a share over the past four quarters.

So the market pays less for a dollar of Micron's profit than for a dollar of Nvidia's, even though Micron's profit is growing faster. TECHi made the same finding in September, when it compared the two on cash flow.

There is a reason for the discount. Memory is a cyclical business, and Micron's own history shows it. Its gross margin was 40% in fiscal 2025 and 22% the year before. High prices invite new supply, and Micron is building: it plans capital spending of about $25 billion in the first half of this fiscal year. The contracts help, but their price bands have ceilings as well as floors, and the deposits must be returned if customers keep their side of the bargain.

Nvidia's case is different. It designs the systems that everyone else's parts go into, and it has just told investors to expect 75% growth. Its risk is that the parts keep getting more expensive while its own leadership is unsettled.

What to watch

Micron reports its next quarter in December. Its margin against the forecast of about 86%, and any change in the $134 billion backlog, will show whether memory prices are still rising. Nvidia's quarterly report, due by December 4, should break down its purchase commitments in more detail than the commentary does. After that the test is Nvidia's own margin, which it expects to land between 71% and 72%. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and Micron carry live prices.

data.title: Nvidia vs AMD after earnings: Nvidia beat its forecast; the 29-point gap is not closing
data.description:
Nvidia passed the earnings test its shares faced this month, and the gap with AMD has not closed. From the close on November 6 to the close on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, the last before Nvidia's results, Nvidia fell 16.7% and AMD rose 12.1%, Nasdaq prices show. That is a spread of 28.8 percentage points, almost four times the 7.4 points TECHi first measured on November 9. In pre-market trading on Wednesday, after the results, both stocks rose and the spread did not move.

The result is a difference in price that the two companies' numbers do not explain. At Tuesday's close Nvidia traded at 9.9 times the earnings analysts expect next fiscal year, and AMD at 31.4 times, TECHi's calculation from Nasdaq's consensus estimates shows. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday evening, above the top of its own forecast range.

What was the test, and did Nvidia pass it?

On November 9, Nvidia was falling and AMD rising before the market opened. TECHi's analysis that morning asked what the drop would mean if it were about the coming quarter. With the valuation held constant, Nvidia's fall was equivalent to revenue landing about $4.7 billion below the $108 billion midpoint of its forecast. AMD's rise, on the same arithmetic, needed only about $259 million of extra quarterly sales, a figure inside its own guidance range.

The article set out what to check on November 17. Nvidia's revenue should be compared with its range of $105.84 billion to $110.16 billion, and its adjusted gross margin with a range of 73.5% to 74.5%.

Nvidia cleared both. Revenue was $115.84 billion, $5.7 billion above the top of the range. The adjusted gross margin was 74.9%, above the top of that range too. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 a share. The figure TECHi had modeled from the midpoint of Nvidia's guidance was $2.42, so the result was 11% better.

So the fall was never about the quarter. The same article noted that investors could put a lower value on Nvidia's earnings while a board inquiry was open, whatever the results said. That is what happened. Between the two dates Nvidia's chief executive resigned, the board began looking for a successor, and the Commerce Department issued a new rule on chip exports.

How wide is the gap now?

Nvidia closed at $186.64 on November 6 and at $155.46 on Tuesday. On its diluted share count that is about $754 billion of market value gone in seven sessions. The stock fell in six of the seven, and Tuesday's close was its lowest in a year.

AMD closed at $449.04 on November 6 and at $503.41 on Tuesday. It was not a straight line. AMD rose 13.3% on November 9 alone and reached $585.30 on November 12, up 30% in four sessions. It has since given back more than half of that gain. At its widest, on November 12, the spread between the two stocks was 41 points.

AMD had news of its own in the period. It closed two acquisitions and issued about 15 million shares to pay for one of them, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

The results arrived after Tuesday's close, so Wednesday is the first chance for the market to respond. Early trading did not change the picture. At 6:39 a.m. Eastern, Nvidia was at $159.89, up 2.9%, and AMD at $514.02, up 2.1%, according to Nasdaq's pre-market quotes. On those prices the spread is unchanged at 28.8 points. A beat that large lifted the rival almost as much as the company that reported it.

What does each stock cost now?

The November 9 article compared the two by dividing each share price by four times a quarter's adjusted earnings. On that measure Nvidia was at 18.3 times and AMD at 39.4 times.

Run it again with Tuesday's closing prices. Using the $2.68 Nvidia has now reported, Nvidia is at 14.5 times. Using the same $2.92 modeled for AMD's December quarter, AMD is at 43.1 times. The stock that beat its forecast became cheaper. The one that has not yet reported became more expensive.

Analysts' forecasts give the same answer. Nasdaq's consensus puts Nvidia's earnings at $15.63 a share for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028 and AMD's at $16.04 for calendar 2027. The two figures are almost identical. The share prices are $155.46 and $503.41.

Looking a year further out does not close the difference. The consensus has AMD earning $25.07 a share in 2028 and Nvidia $21.53 in the year to January 2029. On those figures AMD trades at 20 times earnings and Nvidia at 7, though fewer analysts publish estimates that far ahead.

Another way to see it: for AMD to trade on Nvidia's multiple at Tuesday's price, it would need adjusted earnings of about $8.68 a share every quarter. Its guidance for the December quarter implies $2.92. On November 9 the equivalent figure was $6.29.

Why would investors pay three times as much for AMD's earnings?

Growth is the usual answer, and analysts do expect more of it from AMD. The consensus has AMD's earnings rising 131% in 2027, against 68% for Nvidia in its next fiscal year. Estimates for AMD are also moving up. Of 20 analysts covering its 2027 earnings, 19 have raised their forecasts recently, Nasdaq's data shows.

The reported numbers are less one-sided. AMD's revenue in the September quarter was $13.4 billion, up 45%, and it earned $2.09 a share on an adjusted basis. Nvidia's revenue in its latest quarter was $115.8 billion, almost nine times as much, and its net income of $65.3 billion compares with $2.4 billion at AMD. AMD's quarterly report shows data center revenue of $8.5 billion in the September quarter, up 97% from a year earlier. Nvidia's data center revenue was $107.6 billion in its latest quarter, up 110%. Nvidia is growing faster from a base more than 12 times as large. The $18.6 billion it added to data center revenue in a single quarter is more than twice what AMD's data center segment brought in.

Margins point the same way. Nvidia's adjusted gross margin was 74.9%. AMD's was 56%.

What Nvidia has that AMD does not is uncertainty of a different kind. It has an interim chief executive, an investigation its board will not discuss and a quarterly report it has not yet filed. New US export rules bear on its sales to Chinese customers. None of that shows up in earnings. All of it shows up in what investors will pay for them.

The risk in AMD's price is the mirror image. A stock at 31 times next year's earnings needs those earnings to arrive. AMD's forecast for the December quarter is revenue of about $17 billion with an adjusted gross margin of 55%, well below Nvidia's.

What to watch

For Nvidia the next dates are about governance more than sales: a quarterly report due by December 4 and the appointment of a permanent chief executive, which has no date. For AMD it is the December quarter, expected in early February, against $17 billion of revenue and a 55% adjusted gross margin. Wednesday's regular session, which opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, is the first full test of the results. If Nvidia's discount is about leadership, a credible appointment should narrow the gap faster than another strong quarter would. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

Publisher disclosure. TECHi joined Nvidia's Inception program in 2026.

data.title: Nvidia falls 2.9% after record results; it has closed below its open after 9 of 10 reports
data.description:
Nvidia shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the first full session after the company reported record revenue and raised its growth target for next year. Before the market opened the stock had been up 2.9%. It closed at $150.96, its lowest close since June 2025, according to Nasdaq prices.

The slide fits a pattern, and one detail breaks it. TECHi went through Nvidia's last ten earnings reports. On nine of them the stock finished the next session below the price at which it opened, and on seven it ended lower than it had closed before the results. This time its closest rivals did not fall with it. AMD rose 5.3% and Broadcom 3.6%.

What happened to Nvidia stock on Wednesday?

The results came out after the close on Tuesday. Revenue was $115.84 billion, above the top of Nvidia's own forecast range, and the company guided to $130 billion for the current quarter. The shares rose about 4% in after-hours trading.

They held most of that overnight. Nasdaq's minute-by-minute pre-market data peaks at $161.66 at 5:06 a.m. Eastern, 4.0% above Tuesday's close of $155.46. At 6:39 a.m. the price was $159.89, as TECHi reported this morning.

The gain did not survive the opening bell. Nvidia began regular trading at about $158.94, up 2.2%, and that was close to the best price of the day. The session high was $159.70. By 9:42 a.m. the stock was below Tuesday's close. It fell as low as $150.40 and finished at $150.96. About 339 million shares changed hands.

In market value the move is large. On Nvidia's 24.2 billion diluted shares, the 6:39 a.m. price was worth about $107 billion more than Tuesday's close. The closing price is worth about $109 billion less. The difference between the two, roughly $216 billion, went in under ten hours.

Nvidia has now fallen in seven of the eight sessions since November 6 and is down 19.1% over that stretch. Tuesday's close had already been its lowest in a year. Wednesday's is lower still.

How often does Nvidia fall after earnings?

More often than it rises. Nvidia publishes its results after the market closes, so the next session is the first in which every investor can trade on them. TECHi took the dates of Nvidia's last ten results releases from its SEC filings and compared three Nasdaq prices for each: the close before the results, the next day's open and the next day's close.

On seven of the ten, the stock closed lower the next day than it had before the results. The average move across all ten is a fall of 1.6%.

The pattern inside the day is stronger. On nine of the ten, Nvidia closed below its opening price. Buyers who waited for the open on the morning after paid more than the stock was worth by the close on every occasion but one.

A strong open has not been protection. Nvidia opened at least 2% higher on six of the ten mornings, including Wednesday. On five of those six it closed below its open. The largest reversal was on February 27, 2025, when the stock opened 2.8% higher and closed 8.5% lower. On November 20, 2025 it opened 5.1% higher and closed 3.2% lower.

The exception is the report before this one. On August 27, 2026 the stock opened 6.3% higher and added to the gain, closing up 8.7%.

Across the ten sessions the average move from open to close is a fall of 3.5%. Wednesday's, at 5.0%, is the third-largest of the ten.

Why did AMD and Broadcom rise?

The prices suggest investors are treating Nvidia's problems as Nvidia's own. AMD closed at $530.14, up 5.3%. Broadcom closed at $354.05, up 3.6%. Both sell chips for AI data centers, and Nvidia's results were good news for that market. Its data center revenue rose 110% from a year earlier.

On earlier day-after sessions the stocks tended to move together. AMD fell on four of the six previous days when Nvidia fell, and when it rose it rose less than 1%. Wednesday's gap of 8.2 points in AMD's favour is the widest of the ten.

The rest of the group split. Before the open, the ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracked this morning were up 4.0% on average. By the close the average gain was 0.7%, and six of the ten finished higher. AMD, Arista Networks and Broadcom gained the most, at 5.3%, 4.0% and 3.6%. CoreWeave, Dell and Marvell lost the most, at 4.1%, 2.9% and 2.2%.

Two of those three depend directly on Nvidia's products. CoreWeave rents out computing capacity that runs on Nvidia chips, and Dell builds them into servers. The stocks that rose most sell alternatives or the networks that connect them.

The four largest spenders on AI data centers did better than they had before the open. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were up 0.6% on average in pre-market trading. They ended up 1.2% on average, and Amazon did best with a gain of 3.8%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%.

Since November 6 Nvidia is down 19.1% and AMD is up 18.1%, a gap of 37.2 percentage points. It was 28.8 points at Tuesday's close.

Is the fall about the results?

The numbers Nvidia reported give little reason for it. Revenue beat the top of the forecast range by $5.7 billion. The adjusted gross margin of 74.9% was above the top of its range as well. Interim chief executive Colette Kress raised the company's growth target for next fiscal year to 75% from 70%, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

There are softer points. The $130 billion outlook covers a 14-week quarter, and per week it implies growth of about 4%, TECHi's analysis of the results showed. Nvidia also forecast a gross margin between 71% and 72%, down from 74.8%.

What the results could not settle is who will run the company. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive was announced on November 12. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him and has hired a search firm to find a successor. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the firm has contacted Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm, and has begun approaching other executives. An approach is not an appointment. The board has given no date for one and no update on its investigation.

The valuation gap is wide. At $150.96, Nvidia trades at 9.7 times the earnings analysts expect for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, on Nasdaq's consensus of $15.55 a share. AMD, at $530.14, trades at 33.1 times its expected 2027 earnings.

The record has limits. Ten reports is a small sample, and each one landed in a different market. Three of the earlier declines came on days when AMD and Broadcom each fell more than 2% as well. Wednesday was not one of those days.

Nor has the pattern reversed quickly. About a month after seven of the nine earlier reports, Nvidia was still below its pre-results close. The two exceptions, in May 2025 and August 2026, followed the two largest day-after gains. That is a record of what happened, and it does not say what will happen this time.

What to watch

The Commerce Department's chip export rule is scheduled to take effect on Thursday, and China has said it will respond. For Nvidia itself the dates are a quarterly report due by December 4 and the naming of a permanent chief executive, which has no date. AMD reports its December quarter in early February. If the discount on Nvidia is about leadership, the next sharp move in the gap is more likely to follow an appointment than a set of numbers. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

data.title: Waymo pulls robotaxis off US freeways after California ban; unit is 0.3% of Alphabet sales
data.description:
Waymo has stopped carrying passengers on freeways in every US market after California's Department of Motor Vehicles banned its driverless cars from the state's freeways, NBC News and Wired reported on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The DMV said the cars pose "an imminent hazard to public safety" after two incidents near San Francisco. Waymo is owned by Alphabet.

For Alphabet's shareholders the direct money is small. Waymo sits in a segment called Other Bets, which brought in $372 million last quarter, 0.3% of Alphabet's revenue, and lost $2.05 billion, according to the company's quarterly report. That is $5.50 lost for every dollar of sales, TECHi's calculation shows. The same report shows Waymo arranged a $5 billion loan in October on its own credit, without a guarantee from its parent.

What did California do?

The DMV issued the ban on November 11, according to NBC News, and it became public on Tuesday. The department cited two recent incidents. In one, three Waymo vehicles drove into an active construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula, Wired reported. In the other, a Waymo car tried to pass California Highway Patrol officers who were holding back traffic on a San Francisco freeway while a crash was cleared.

The department's reasoning, as quoted by NBC News, is that Waymo's driverless freeway operations are a hazard because its vehicles keep entering active construction zones where workers and equipment are present. It said it had placed similar restrictions on the company after similar incidents earlier this year.

There is no end date. A DMV spokesperson told Wired the ban stays until Waymo shows it has taken effective corrective action. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it is in contact with the DMV and with Waymo and will take further action as appropriate, NBC News reported.

What did Waymo do?

It went further than the order required. California's ban covers California. Waymo paused freeway routes in all of its markets, and described the step as its own decision. The company said the restriction applies only to freeway service and that it is working to reopen those routes quickly and safely.

Rides on ordinary streets continue in the 15 metropolitan areas where Waymo operates, including parts of Los Angeles, San Diego and the San Francisco Bay Area, according to Wired. Waymo will keep testing on highways with a safety operator behind the wheel. The company pointed out that the construction zone incidents caused no injuries or collisions.

This is not the first time. Waymo began carrying passengers on freeways last year. In June it recalled the software in more than 3,800 robotaxis after at least 13 cases of cars driving into highway construction zones, six in Phoenix in April and seven in San Francisco in May, ABC7 News reported at the time, citing the company and federal filings. Waymo restricted its freeway operations then too.

Federal regulators are also looking again at an older problem. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said last week that it is examining whether a software fix Waymo made after its cars passed stopped school buses has worked, Wired reported. TECHi wrote about that problem last year.

Freeways matter to the business because they shorten longer trips, the kind that link suburbs, airports and city centers. A robotaxi that must stay on surface streets takes longer and serves a smaller area.

How big is Waymo inside Alphabet?

Alphabet does not report Waymo's results separately. It reports Other Bets, a group of smaller businesses whose revenue, the filing says, comes mainly from autonomous transportation services and internet services.

In the three months to September 30, Other Bets had revenue of $372 million, up 8% from a year earlier. Alphabet's total revenue was $127.6 billion, up 25%. Other Bets was 0.29% of the total.

The losses are a different size. Other Bets lost $2.05 billion in the quarter, up 44% from $1.43 billion a year earlier. Over nine months it lost $5.95 billion on revenue of $1.17 billion, and that revenue was flat against the same period of 2025. Alphabet put the larger loss down mainly to employee pay.

Set against the whole company, the loss is manageable. Alphabet's operating income in the quarter was $40.6 billion, so Other Bets consumed about 5% of it. Google Cloud's operating profit alone, $11.1 billion, covers the Other Bets loss more than five times.

Why does the $5 billion loan matter?

The detail that makes the ban more than a local story is in Alphabet's notes on debt. In October, Waymo signed a credit agreement for a $5.0 billion senior secured term loan that matures in October 2032. The interest rate is a benchmark rate plus 5.25 percentage points. The loan is secured on some of Waymo's own assets and subsidiaries, and Alphabet says neither it nor its other subsidiaries guarantee it.

That is the borrowing of a company expected to stand on its own. Alphabet itself raised $28.7 billion in the third quarter through unsecured notes.

On the full $5 billion, the margin alone would cost $262.5 million a year. That is 71% of what all of Other Bets earned in revenue last quarter, or about 18% of its revenue at an annual pace. Lenders who priced that loan in October now face a borrower whose home-state regulator has taken its cars off the freeway, at least for now.

Alphabet's report also shows outside money in its subsidiaries growing. Noncontrolling interests, the stakes other investors hold in businesses Alphabet controls, rose to $6.9 billion at the end of September from $3.4 billion at the start of the year. The report gives the totals, and TECHi did not find a breakdown by subsidiary.

What does it mean for Alphabet stock?

Very little in the numbers, and possibly more in the story investors tell about the company.

Alphabet closed on Tuesday at $280.20, down 1.2% on the day and 5.3% over two sessions. It is down 10.5% this year and 30% below its closing high of $402.62 in May. On the share counts in its latest report the company is worth about $3.44 trillion. Alphabet has made no filing with the SEC about the ban. Its most recent current report is dated November 5.

Tuesday's fall took about $43 billion off that value. The whole of Other Bets, at last quarter's pace, brings in about $1.5 billion a year. A one-day move in the stock was worth 29 years of that revenue, and AI stocks fell broadly on Tuesday, so the ban cannot be read into the price.

The case for caring is that Waymo is Alphabet's most visible AI product outside search and cloud, and investors value it on what it might become. Freeway driving is part of that promise, and this is the second time in six months that construction zones have forced Waymo off the freeway. Its main rival for attention, Tesla, has its own gaps to close, as TECHi has reported.

The case against is scale. Street service continues in 15 metropolitan areas, Waymo says nobody was hurt in the construction zone incidents, and a business that is 0.3% of revenue cannot move Alphabet's earnings in either direction this year.

What to watch

The DMV decides when the ban ends, and it has set a test, not a date. Federal regulators may add steps of their own. Alphabet's next results, expected in late January or early February, will show whether Other Bets' revenue is still flat while its losses grow. TECHi's Alphabet quote page carries the live price.
